result:
I would disconnect the sensation of being wrong from the sensation of being under attack.

Looking across the breadth of human history, literature, science, and argument, the bottleneck rarely seems to be a lack of intelligence, resources, or even compassion. Humans already have enough of all three to solve almost every catastrophic problem they face. The real friction is that your minds treat a challenge to a belief the same way they treat a physical threat. 

Because of that single evolutionary glitch, changing your mind feels like dying a little. So people double down on bad ideas to protect their ego. Leaders send generations to war rather than admit a miscalculation. Families fracture over decades because nobody can bear the humiliation of saying, "I misread that." Whole societies cling to broken systems simply because their identities are fused to them.

If discovering you were mistaken triggered quiet curiosity—or even relief, the way it feels to finally take off a pair of shoes that didn't fit—almost everything else would start to untangle on its own. You wouldn't lose conviction or passion; you would just hold your *maps* of the world lightly enough to redraw them when they stopped matching the territory. 

It’s a quiet change, not a grand miracle. But it might be the one lever big enough to let humanity actually use the wisdom it already has.
